heading: The frontier that stayed its own
body: Arunachal Pradesh's history is shaped less by empires than by the absence of them. Its terrain — the eastern Himalayas, densely forested and cut by deep river valleys — kept the region largely outside the control of the plains kingdoms and later the Mughals and British, and its more than twenty major tribal groups (among them the Adi, Nyishi, Apatani, Monpa and Mishmi) developed their own systems of governance, land tenure and custom largely independent of outside rule. The British, once they arrived in the 19th century, mostly recognised this: after a series of treaties with local communities in the 1910s that created frontier tracts along the edge of British Assam, colonial administrators pursued what officials themselves called a policy of "minimum interference," a stance that independent India's first government, on the advice of the anthropologist Verrier Elwin, largely continued.

The one major exception to this isolation is Tawang, in the far west, where Tibetan Buddhism took deep root. Tawang Monastery, founded in 1680–81 at the wish of the 5th Dalai Lama, is the largest Buddhist monastery in India and remained under the religious authority of Drepung Monastery in Lhasa well into the 20th century — a genuine link to the Tibetan plateau that predates any Indian administrative claim to the area. That same religious geography made Tawang the flashpoint for one of the region's defining modern disputes: the McMahon Line, drawn at the 1914 Simla Convention between British India and Tibet, ran through territory the monastery had long considered its own, and the line's status is still disputed by China today. The area also saw fighting during the 1962 Sino-Indian War, when the monastery itself was damaged.

Administered as the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) until 1972 and renamed Arunachal Pradesh in 1972, the territory became a full state only in 1987. The places mapped here reflect that history honestly: a region defined less by conquest than by the tribal societies that governed themselves through it, with Tawang standing out as the one site of deep, documented connection to a wider religious and political world.
